newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end higher led by platinum.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end higher led by platinum.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended higher Monday, led by platinum and palladium, as the complex continued last week's recovery.
"Platinum and palladium had the best close and hopefully this might rub off on gold tomorrow," North American Equity Services COMEX floor trader John Geraghty said.
COMEX April gold ended up $1.10 an ounce at $355.50, but had yet to test Friday's highs at $356.80.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $353.00/50, compared to the London Monday afternoon fix at $353.05 and the New York close Friday at $351.90/40.

In data published Monday, COMEX gold open interest fell a further 3,510 contracts Friday to 183,576 lots, a fall of 16,142 lots in the past week, suggesting the rally was being driven by short covering by funds, traders said.

April gold's five-day simple moving average has crossed back above its 21-day average for the first time since November 1996, but remains below its 55-day average, with resistance now seen around $360 an ounce, traders said.
But physical demand for gold is running at high levels also, as Mid-East and Asian investors take advantage of lower prices, analysts said.
Gold imports in Dubai soared to a record 46.36 tonnes in January, a 92.6 percent increase over January 1996, according to the World Gold Council.
Premiums for ten-tola bars and kilobars edged higher in the Dubai entrepot, which traditionally supplies other mid-eastern and Indian markets.

The upcoming Indian wedding season and end-of-March Dubai Shopping Festival are seen partly behind the demand for gold in Dubai, along with the recent move by India to deregulate its gold market, allowing non-resident Indian imports to double to 10 kilograms per person.
Signs that the long rally in the US dollar against yen and mark may be topping out may also be helping gold, analysts said.
The dollar's rise to 48 month highs against the yen in the past year helped depress gold demand, with Japanese gold imports down 48 percent in 1996 to 134.4 tonnes.

But "any meaningful upturn in investor demand for gold will remain limited by low inflationary expectations, a strong dollar and attractive returns offered by equity markets," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said.
COMEX March silver closed up 1.0 cent at $5.195 an ounce, though the contract is still consolidating in a $5.140-$5.275 range, after silver initially led the recovery in the precious metals complex.
The spot/gold silver ratio edged up to 67.8 Monday, after seeing a 21-month low at 65.6 a week ago.
NYMEX April platinum ended up $3.90 an ounce at $377.50, after seeing a 10-week high at $379.50 intraday.
The April NYMEX platinum/COMEX gold spread widened to $22.20 an ounce, after dipping back below $20.00 last week.
NYMEX June palladium, now the active contract, ended up $1.35 at $142.25, after equalling the contract high at $143.50 seen on February 13.
In the physical market, palladium sponge remained at a $5.00-6.00 differential to palladium plate, reflecting supply difficulties and rising demand, traders said.

Russian exports of platinum group metals are expected to be much lower in 1997 than in 1996 and no palladium will be exported to Japan in March, a spokesman for Russia's platinum group metals export agency, Almaz, said Monday.
The Russian/Japanese palladium supply contract talks broke down last December and were due to resume in March, but Monday the Almaz spokesman said he now did not know when the talks would resume.
Russia accounts for about 60 pct of world palladium supply, and Japan accounts for about 40 pct of world demand.
